title: One Report Closed Over a Hundred Medical Schools, and Black Doctors Were Cut Off
dek: The Flexner Report is often written as the starting point of medical education modernization, but it also closed five of seven Black medical schools, and for nearly forty years no new Black medical school appeared.
why: Medium information density; the first half is a chronological account of Flexner's life, and the real value is in the second half: how the report reshaped medical education and how it cut off the supply of Black doctors.
who: Listeners interested in the history of medical education, the history of racial inequality in the United States, and how professional associations reshape an industry through standard-setting; anyone who wants to understand why "standardization" can eliminate disadvantaged institutions along with it.
skip: The first ten minutes or so of chronological detail about Flexner's life and family, and the sponsor break in the middle.

points.h: The report's author was not a doctor but an education reformer
points.body: Abraham Flexner was not part of the medical establishment. In 1890 he ran an experimental school with no fixed curriculum, no exams, and no grades, and its students still got into good schools; in 1908 he wrote The American College, A Criticism, attacking American higher education, which led Henry Smith Pritchett of the Carnegie Foundation to approach him and ask him to look at medical schools in the United States and Canada with the same critical eye. He spent two years visiting 155 medical schools, recording each one's admission requirements, faculty, finances, laboratories, and hospital affiliations, and in 1910 delivered Medical Education in the United States and Canada. Precisely because he was an outsider rather than a member of the medical community, the assessment dared to be merciless.

points.h: Medical schools were still teaching outdated knowledge
points.body: In the fifty years before the report, bacteriology, diagnostic techniques, and surgery were changing rapidly, but medical schools had no uniform standards. At many schools the faculty were practicing physicians who taught the way they themselves had been taught and did not update the content. The result was that the care doctors gave patients was, at best, outdated and, at worst, life-threatening. Admission standards were equally chaotic: when the report was published, 74% of medical schools required only a high school diploma, some accepted even a high school equivalency certificate, only one-fifth required more than two years of college coursework, and many schools were essentially for-profit businesses.

points.h: He recommended closing 120 of the 155 schools
points.body: Flexner first set standards and then graded each school: admission should require college-level biology, chemistry, and physics; the curriculum should include classroom and laboratory work in anatomy, pathology, bacteriology, and pharmacology; there should be a teaching hospital for practical training; and teachers should be salaried, full-time faculty doing teaching and research, not part-time practicing physicians. He published the results by state and by school, naming dirty laboratories and lax standards, and criticizing course schedules that left students sitting for hours listening to dull lectures by part-time instructors. In the end he recommended closing 120 of the 155 schools. Within a decade the number of American medical schools was only half of what it had been, the surviving schools reformed their standards and curricula, and laboratory and clinical teaching were substantially modernized. In Canada only one school appeared on the recommended closure list, and it ultimately did not close.

points.h: He never reckoned with the Black medical schools' books
points.body: The report was equally merciless toward Black medical schools, writing that five of the seven could "make no valuable contribution at this time," and affirming only Howard and Meharry as worth developing. But the assessment did not take into account that Black medical schools charged far lower tuition than white schools, had smaller endowments, and already operated on extremely thin margins. He wrote that "the Negro needs good schools rather than many schools," and said that one of the most important duties of Black doctors and Black nurses was to teach hygiene rather than life-saving skills—a statement that is itself racist. Every Black medical school he named as inadequate closed: the first four closed before 1914, the fifth in 1915, and the last held on until 1923.

points.h: The next Black medical school would not come until 1966
points.body: Howard and Meharry remained, and still exist today. But the next medical school primarily serving Black students was Charles R. Drew Medical School in Los Angeles, which did not open until 1966 and was created in response to the Black community's need for medical access; the one after that was Morehouse School of Medicine in Atlanta in 1975. The direct consequence of narrowing the options was a huge care gap: many potential doctors were excluded from educational opportunity because of geography, and Black patients were often cared for by white doctors who, even at best, carried inherent racial bias. A panel convened by the AMA Institute for Ethics in 2005 concluded that Flexner's phrase "good schools rather than many schools" ensured that medicine remained segregated, and that the communities most in need of doctors were the ones left without them.

points.h: The AMA was paying behind Carnegie's project
points.body: One fact not disclosed at the time: the Carnegie Foundation hired Flexner for the project, and the AMA was also a sponsor. There is also an unresolved question—whether someone connected to the AMA accompanied him on some of the school visits. He gave differing accounts at different times, sometimes saying the person accompanied him, and later changing his story to say they merely met there, so whether the report was subject to more direct directional influence remains impossible to determine.

points.h: Did he know he was limiting Black medicine?
points.body: He knew. The report contains an idealistic passage saying that building up Howard and Meharry would benefit the nation far more than barely sustaining more schools. In 1933 he wrote to the board of the institute he had founded, arguing that hiring and admissions "shall not directly or indirectly take race, religion, or sex into consideration." One explanation comes from biographer Thomas Neville Bonner: when Flexner was growing up in Louisville, the local Black community had more services and opportunities than in many places, with more than a dozen Black schools and vocational training in medicine and law for Black students; the Flexner family was not wealthy, there were Black families among the neighbors, and he and his siblings often played with Black children in the community. This may have made him overly idealistic about the reality of Black family life, and he later admitted that only when he began studying educational institutions did he realize how disadvantaged those Black classmates of his had been.

points.h: The hygiene line may not have been his own
points.body: The claim that hygiene was the main duty of Black doctors is one of the key pieces of evidence for judging Flexner racist. But the leaders of Meharry and Howard said similar things in 1907 and 1908—two or three years before the report—and those leaders were also white. This suggests Flexner's wording may have been a restatement of the schools' established mission rather than an independent judgment of his own. In 2011 Lynn E. Miller and Richard M. Weiss, in the Journal of the History of Medicine and Allied Sciences, proposed another possibility: that this language was actually opening up a public health role for the doctors at these schools in order to win support across racial divides—because those statements about hygiene being the most urgent need were immediately followed by the conclusion that these institutions obviously deserved support. The AMA issued a public apology in 2008 for its history of racial inequality.
